content:
A federal judge ordered the Trump administration to provide 30 days' notice to the court before proposing any changes to existing construction plans at the Kennedy Center — including "demolition."

The order largely reaffirmed the terms of a previous injunction barring the government from closing or altering the building. It came as officials worked to shut down and potentially demolish the presidential memorial and performing arts venue, after a court ordered President Trump's name removed from the building.

The president told reporters on Wednesday that the building could be "knocked down" if his name wasn't added back in some form.

Then, late Wednesday night, Trump was photographed on Air Force One looking at an image that appeared to show the Kennedy Center demolished, with the words "KENNEDY CENTER DEMOLISHED."

The text was partially obscured, visible through the lettering on a window of the aircraft. Trump appeared in an adjacent window, seemingly looking at the sign.

In his Thursday order, Judge Charles Cooper authorized Ohio Democratic Rep. Joyce Beatty — a Kennedy Center trustee and plaintiff in the case — to conduct discovery into the photograph of Trump looking at the image.

The Ohio Democrat has led the charge against Trump's takeover of the revered arts institution and the "unlawful" closure of the venue honoring former President John F. Kennedy.

The Kennedy Center's board, stocked with Trump's own appointees, voted Tuesday to close the center for up to two years for $257 million in renovations.

Beatty requested an emergency hearing after the closure was announced, and filed supplemental documents after the photograph surfaced Thursday.

The latest filing said: "A photograph circulating on social media shows President Trump on Air Force One looking at a sign that appears to read 'Kennedy Center DEMOLISHED.'" It included an enlarged version of the image.

Beatty's attorneys argued in court filings that closing the Kennedy Center was a "transparent pretext" to justify shuttering it permanently. "The facts before the Court are deeply concerning."

They asked the judge to make clear that his previous order "prohibits demolishing the building."

Kennedy Center President and Chief Operating Officer Matt Floca said in a filing the center submitted itself on Thursday that the temporary closure was due to "ongoing structural deterioration caused by an aging building that poses serious safety risks to the public."

The center, established by Congress and opened in 1971, is currently closed outside of normal operating hours.
